_readme: The hand-written part of voice-guide's schematic: levels 1 to 3, their walk-throughs and the design considerations. The class level is generated from the Go code into classes/*.json by cmd/classgen, which scripts/schematic.sh runs, and never written here. How to update it: the schematic skill.

considerations: one entry per design decision from docs/reference/architecture.md that a level shows, keyed by a slug; one no view, card or edge cites is removed. The page lists them folded away under a level, a card or a connection, each title linking to 'ref', the design's anchor, under 'design' (the design's address online), with its decision beneath. Fields: title (the decision's title), ref, section (where it sits in the design), status (accepted, proposed or deferred), decision and why (one or two plain sentences each), tradeoff or rejected (one short line); section, status, why, tradeoff and rejected are kept for whoever edits this file and not shown.

views: one per level shown. View fields: id, title, level (1 to 4), lead (the panel's opening paragraph), start (the top level only: two lines over the canvas saying what it shows and to try a walk-through, a line break between them), considerations (ids), flows (the walk-throughs, below), nodes and edges (hand-written levels), classes (the id of the class view a level-3 view links to), and for a class view type ('classes'), source (its generated file under classes/) and root (its module's root package).

views: one per level. A view lists its nodes and edges and the considerations that shape it. Node fields: id, kind (client, service, module, core, shared, port, adapter, store, external, group), name, path, tech, summary (on the card, keep it under ~110 characters), description (the side panel), why (where it matters: one plain sentence on why the card is built this way, from the design's reasoning, shown in the panel above its decisions), setting (on a card a setting switches: one line, the setting's name, a colon, then its choices joined by ' · ', or a range or a phrase, such as 'VOICE_TTS: kokoro · fake'; drawn as a chip on the card, and in the panel with where it is set, .env for a name in upper case, the agent's file for one in lower case; one per card, the most useful), considerations (ids), drill (a view id opened by double-click), focus (for a class view, the package to fit on), parent (a group node's id; groups come before their children), context (true for a node from outside the level, drawn faded), tag (core, inbound, outbound, entry point), members (a port's methods; a card shows the first few, the panel all).

Edge fields: from, to, protocol (a short chip such as HTTP or WebRTC), send (what the caller sends, under ~60 characters), back (what comes back), detail (the side panel), style (flow by default; implements for an adapter satisfying a port), considerations. Every label was checked against the adapters in the code; keep it that way.

flows: each hand-written level with cards has two to four walk-throughs, named stories the reader steps through or plays in order. A flow has id, name (what happens, in plain words, such as 'You say something') and steps; a step has nodes and edges (ids from its own view, which it lights while the rest dims; a connection's two cards are always among its nodes) and caption (one plain sentence, ideally under ~150 characters: who does what to whom, read from the code and the design, in the design's terms, with no design labels and no vendor names, which belong on a card's tech line). The data tests check every id and that every level with cards has a flow.

Folding is drawn, not written: at a level, each adapter folds behind the cards it plugs into (the ports it implements or, failing those, the core types it calls), and an outside card only folded adapters reach folds with it; a click on the host shows them. A walk-through shows every card it names, folded or not. Nothing in this file says what folds; draw implements edges and an inbound adapter's call into its core as usual.

omitted: Go packages under internal/ and cmd/ deliberately drawn nowhere, each with why; the fakes among them, since the levels show what runs, not the shortcuts the tests take. Every other package (but the code sqlc generates, the db folders) is named by some node's path, or matched by a path with a * in it; cmd/classgen's tests check that, and that every package a path names exists.

importedFreely, on a level-2 node: a package of plain types every part may import, such as the caller, so its imports aren't drawn. Otherwise every import from one part at level 2 to another needs an edge between them, either way; cmd/voice, which wires everything, is exempt. cmd/classgen's tests check that too.

one-service-four-modules.title: One service with four fenced modules
one-service-four-modules.section: How it works · Modules and boundaries
one-service-four-modules.decision: Conversation, speech, user context and agents are modules of one Go service with hard boundaries, and the service scales by running more copies of itself. Speech calls conversation and never the reverse; conversation reaches user context only through its service.
one-service-four-modules.why: One deployable is the simplest to build, run and measure, and enforced boundaries keep each module's data and rules in one place.
one-service-four-modules.tradeoff: A boundary inside one process can be crossed by mistake, so depguard checks it on every push; moving a module out later is a refactor, not a setting.

swap-points.title: Every component behind a swap point
swap-points.section: How it works · Modules and boundaries
swap-points.decision: Each speech stage, model access and storage sits behind an interface owned by the module that uses it, with the implementation chosen by configuration. Only the adapter imports a vendor's package, and every port has a fake from its first day.
swap-points.why: Speech and model vendors change fast in price, speed and terms; swapping one should touch one adapter and one setting.
swap-points.tradeoff: An interface per seam and adapters to maintain, so a vendor gets one only where a second real implementation is planned.

hexagonal.title: Hexagonal inside each module
hexagonal.section: How it works · Modules and boundaries
hexagonal.decision: Each module's core holds its rules and declares what it needs as small interfaces, its ports. Inbound adapters (the HTTP API) call the core; outbound adapters (WebRTC, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, the model, storage, fakes) implement a port, and the entry point wires them in.
hexagonal.why: A component is switched by changing one adapter and one setting, and Go places an interface in the package that uses it, which is where a port lives.
hexagonal.tradeoff: More small packages, and a wiring step at startup.

one-account.title: One user account; records owned by the workspace holding them
one-account.decision: A user has one account across voice-guide, and every record about them names the workspace holding it; by default only that workspace's agents read it.
one-account.why: The same model serves a workspace open to anyone and a company serving its own users, and the user, not the workspace, decides what leaves a workspace.
one-account.tradeoff: Sharing context with another workspace needs a grant flow before it works.

go.title: Go for the core service
go.decision: The service that holds the four modules is written in Go.
go.why: Goroutines suit many long-lived audio connections, WebRTC exists in pure Go (Pion), and each service ships as one static binary.

postgres.title: PostgreSQL 18, the only data store at first
postgres.decision: Plain tables for the core, JSON columns for per-agent records and pgvector for relevance search, all in PostgreSQL 18.
postgres.why: One relational store until a measured need for another; version 18 for native UUIDv7.
postgres.rejected: A wide-column store for turns from the start, or a separate vector store; both are later paths.

sqlc.title: sqlc with pgx for queries; goose for migrations
sqlc.decision: Queries are written as SQL, checked and turned into typed Go by sqlc and run with pgx; migrations are plain SQL files run by goose.
sqlc.why: SQL stays SQL and is checked against the migrations at build time.

uuidv7.title: UUIDv7 for every ID
uuidv7.decision: Every stored ID is a UUIDv7; a request ID, chosen by the caller only to recognise a repeat, may be any version.
uuidv7.why: No central counter, so any instance or store creates IDs, and they are time-ordered, so turns read in order.

react.title: React with TypeScript in the browser, calling the Go service directly
react.decision: The web page is React with TypeScript and calls the Go service directly, with no layer in between.
react.why: The standard web stack, and no layer in between until one has a job.
react.rejected: A backend-for-frontend now: a hop and a service before it has a job.

language-per-library.title: Python for the speech-to-text service; TypeScript for the model service
language-per-library.decision: Each side service is written in the language its key library ships in: Moonshine for speech-to-text, the Claude Agent SDK for the model.
language-per-library.why: There is no subscription route to the model from Go, and Moonshine ships for Python.

containers.title: Every part in a container; settings from the environment
containers.decision: Docker compose runs everything locally and the same containers run in the cloud, with settings from the environment. Compose runs PostgreSQL, Kokoro and the speech-to-text service so far; each other service joins when it gets its container.
containers.why: One way to run everything, so local runs predict cloud runs.
containers.rejected: Tools installed on the machine outside containers.

api-for-products.title: An API for outside products; voice-guide's own web page is its first client
api-for-products.decision: Every endpoint and message is designed for a product outside voice-guide to call; voice-guide's own web page uses only that API, and so does the drop-in client, a custom element in the product's own page. The page and the element hold a session with the same code, written without React.
api-for-products.why: An API used only by its own screen drifts toward that screen. In the product's page, not a frame, the microphone prompt names the product's site; the ticket goes through join(), never an attribute recorders copy.
api-for-products.tradeoff: The page can't take shortcuts, and since it reaches voice through its dev server's proxy, only the drop-in client makes the cross-origin calls a product's page makes.

http-and-webrtc.title: HTTP for agents and sessions, WebRTC for audio
http-and-webrtc.decision: Agents, starting and ending sessions and typed turns go over HTTP, the reply streamed back as server-sent events. A session's audio connection is set up with one WHIP-shaped request, and while it is open, typed turns travel on its data channel so the server playing the reply takes them.
http-and-webrtc.why: Request and reply suit sessions, live audio needs WebRTC, and turns on the data channel reach the server that plays the reply with no messages passed between servers.

problem-details.title: Errors as problem details; the version in the path
problem-details.decision: Every error is an RFC 9457 problem details document, with a type of its own only where a client must tell two errors with one status apart, such as a session that has ended; every path starts with /v1/.
problem-details.why: Products' tools already read the IETF's standard error format, and a version in the path is the easiest to see, route and test.
problem-details.tradeoff: A breaking change means serving two versions side by side for a while.

workspace-every-record.title: Workspace on every record, user on every record about one; every query filters by workspace but the system's sweeps and the key check
workspace-every-record.decision: Every stored record carries its workspace, every record about a user carries the user too, and every query filters by workspace, except the system's own sweeps (ending idle sessions, claiming background jobs, deleting old ones), which find their rows by one condition across workspaces, and the product key check, which finds a key by its hash, since the key is what names the workspace.
workspace-every-record.why: Adding a tenant key after launch means rewriting data access.
workspace-every-record.tradeoff: Until row-level security arrives with a second workspace, a query that forgets the filter is caught only in review.

timed-by-stage.title: Every turn timed by stage
timed-by-stage.decision: Every turn records how long each stage took and which implementation served it; reports give the median and 90th percentile per stage, and the slowest stage is worked on first. The page times what the user feels as well.
timed-by-stage.why: 'Faster' means nothing without a split by stage, and a target set before measuring is a guess.
timed-by-stage.tradeoff: Timing code on every turn, and no number to hold a change against until a target is set.

stateless.title: No conversation held in a server's memory
stateless.decision: Any instance can serve any turn: the database is the conversation's source of truth, and a model process kept per session is a disposable cache any instance can rebuild. A dropped audio connection reconnects to any instance.
stateless.why: State held on one machine can't spread across servers and is lost when that machine restarts.
stateless.tradeoff: Each turn reads the conversation from the database or a cache instead of trusting memory.

background-jobs.title: Slow work as background jobs, in one PostgreSQL queue for every kind
background-jobs.decision: Work longer than a turn, such as a session's summary, runs as a background job in one jobs table for every kind: each kind's inputs are one JSON value only its handler reads. A module queues its job in the same write that calls for it, and a job may wait for another queued with it. Each instance runs a runner per group of kinds, each claiming only its own, so one slow group holds up no other.
background-jobs.why: A turn's time is the product. One queue keeps the claiming, the lease and the retries written and tested once, and queuing in the same write means a job exists exactly when its cause commits.
background-jobs.tradeoff: The database doesn't check a job's inputs, its kind's Go type does; a job runs at least once, not exactly once.
background-jobs.rejected: River, a queue in Redis, a goroutine, a table per kind.

reference-agent.title: The reference agent: a mock interviewer
reference-agent.decision: The first agent practises job interviews: one question at a time about the user's resume, which the product sends as session context, ending with a short summary of weak spots.
reference-agent.why: A real, demanding conversation that exercises every speech stage with the simplest context.
reference-agent.tradeoff: Features other agents need, such as documents or grading, wait for those agents.

agent-versions.title: Agents stored as versions that never change, published from one file per agent
agent-versions.decision: An agent's versions are database rows that are never changed; a change is saved as the next number. New sessions get the newest version and a running session keeps its own, and publishing from agents/<name>.md is a step of its own, never part of a start.
agent-versions.why: Any instance may serve a session's next turn, so every instance must find the exact version the session started on, even mid-deploy.
agent-versions.tradeoff: The file shows only the text it will publish next; earlier versions live in the database.

warm-cache.title: An agent that opens warms the model's cache with its opening
warm-cache.decision: An agent set to open speaks first: the page sends its opening, the session's first turn with no words, and the model writes the greeting from a fixed cue. Every later prompt holds the cue and the greeting byte for byte, so the opening warms the cache; an agent that waits gets no warm-up for now.
warm-cache.why: The opening is a request the session wants anyway, so the warm-up costs nothing more, and it comes once the user can hear it.
warm-cache.tradeoff: An agent that waits pays the full read on the user's first turn; a session left before the user speaks still costs the opening.

product-context.title: The product sends what it knows when a session starts, and what its screen shows with each turn
product-context.decision: Session context, such as a resume, arrives as named text blocks from the product's server, which starts the session with its key, so the user can't change it, and sits in the cached part of the prompt; screen input arrives with each turn. User context holds only what voice-guide learns itself.
product-context.why: The product is the source of truth for its users and its screen; a second copy in voice-guide would drift.
product-context.tradeoff: A product with no store of its own must keep, or resend, what it knows each session.

session-end.title: A session ends when the user ends it, or after five minutes idle
session-end.decision: A session ends once: when the product ends it, or after five minutes with no turn started and none of the user's speech heard. Every instance sweeps once a minute, and an ended session takes no turns and gets no audio connection.
session-end.why: A closed tab never presses End and a page can't reliably say it is closing, so a time limit kept by the server is the only guarantee.
session-end.tradeoff: A user who steps away for five minutes finds the session over, and every turn writes the session's row as well as its own.

speculative-start.title: Start the model before the end of turn is confirmed
speculative-start.decision: Send the turn to the model as soon as the final text is in, while the end-of-turn check runs, and cancel it if the user keeps talking.
speculative-start.why: The check and the rest of the pause would overlap the model's first word instead of adding to it.
speculative-start.tradeoff: Deferred after measuring: the check answered before the final text in every turn but one, so there was nothing to overlap.

webrtc-in-go.title: Audio over WebRTC, in the Go service
webrtc-in-go.decision: Audio travels between browser and server over WebRTC, with Pion in the Go service as the other participant. The server that answers a session's audio connection holds it, one per session there, and a browser whose connection drops opens a new one with any server.
webrtc-in-go.why: The browser removes the agent's echo from the microphone only for audio arriving over WebRTC, and interrupting needs the microphone open while the agent speaks.
webrtc-in-go.tradeoff: More setup than a WebSocket, and some users will need a relay (TURN) server later.

speech-detection.title: Speech detection on the server
speech-detection.decision: Silero VAD runs in pure Go through govad, judging each connection's audio in 32 ms frames: speech starts at a probability of 0.5, a pause is 0.2 s of quiet, the maximum wait 3 s, and 0.2 s of speech over the agent cuts in.
speech-detection.why: It works the same for every client, the server times it, and the build keeps no C library and needs no network hop.
speech-detection.tradeoff: Reacts one hop later than detection in the browser would, and govad has one maintainer.

moonshine.title: Moonshine in a small Python service with OpenAI's realtime transcription API
moonshine.decision: Speech-to-text is Moonshine's streaming English model in a Python service that speaks the part of OpenAI's realtime transcription API voice uses: 24 kHz audio in over a WebSocket, rough text while the user speaks, one final text per utterance.
moonshine.why: Fastest on CPU for live speech by the vendor's figures, it sends text while the user talks, and any service with the same API swaps in by setting.
moonshine.tradeoff: A fourth language and a small service to maintain; Python handles many streams poorly, so scale means more containers.

end-of-turn.title: End of turn: a pause, then Smart Turn, then a maximum wait
end-of-turn.decision: A 0.2 s pause triggers Smart Turn, which judges from the last 8 s of audio whether the user has finished; if not, voice keeps listening up to a 3 s wait. One turn's speech runs to a minute at most.
end-of-turn.why: A silence timer alone either cuts users off or feels slow; judging from the audio pairs with any speech-to-text.
end-of-turn.tradeoff: One more model in the path, and settings to tune per agent.

kokoro.title: Kokoro on the server, short first phrase
kokoro.decision: Text-to-speech is Kokoro on the server's CPU, asked for one phrase at a time as streamed Opus. The first phrase ends at the first punctuation once it holds four words, and each next one is made while the one before plays.
kokoro.why: Free and natural-sounding; Opus straight from Kokoro leaves voice with no audio encoder, and a short first phrase starts the sound sooner.
kokoro.tradeoff: Server CPU per conversation, and on CPU its first audio comes close to the model's first word.

layered-prompt.title: A layered, cached prompt
layered-prompt.decision: The prompt is built in layers, stable ones first: the agent's persona, the session's context, the append-only conversation, then the screen input and the new words. One function renders it from what the session recorded, so every turn and instance produces the same bytes.
layered-prompt.why: Every uncached input token adds to the time to the model's first word, and caching cuts it sharply.
layered-prompt.tradeoff: Changes mid-session must arrive as messages, never as edits to the layers above.

model-access.title: Model access behind a provider-neutral swap point
model-access.decision: voice sends one request per reply (model, the session unless it is an ask outside any session such as a summary, stable layers, conversation, new words) and reads a stream of JSON events back: text, then usage and timing, or an error kind. Which model answers is a setting of the service, recorded with every turn; the model service reaches Claude through its API or the developer's subscription, a setting too.
model-access.why: The subscription is free during development, the API serves anyone with a key, and any model can replace either behind the same interface.
model-access.tradeoff: The subscription route is for the developer alone and must be replaced before anyone else uses voice-guide; the API route bills every turn.

talking-on.title: Talking on after the end of turn: merge, until the agent speaks
talking-on.decision: If the user speaks again after their turn was taken but before any of its reply is heard, the turn is taken back and taken again with all their words as one.
talking-on.why: The user's whole thought reaches the model, and nothing the agent said is lost.
talking-on.tradeoff: Each merge cancels a model request that is partly billed.

cut-in.title: Speech held over the agent cuts in at once; shorter speech over it is passed over
cut-in.decision: A fifth of a second of speech over the agent stops its reply at that moment and becomes the next turn; a click, a breath or a short cough over it is passed over and never sent to the model.
cut-in.why: The agent goes quiet about 0.2 s after the user starts, not after their sentence, the pause and the check.
cut-in.tradeoff: A cough held that long cuts the agent off, and nothing guards against its own voice leaking into the microphone.

heard.title: How much of an interrupted reply was heard
heard.decision: A cut reply counts as heard up to the last audio packet sent before the interrupt, less the round trip and 40 ms for the browser; of the phrase playing, the same share of its text as of its packets. The whole reply is kept with how much of it was heard.
heard.why: The model must not build on words the user never heard.
heard.tradeoff: About a word or two out within a phrase.

declared-context.title: An agent reads only the context kinds it declares
declared-context.decision: User context holds what voice-guide learns about a user (a profile, session summaries); each agent declares the kinds it reads, and a session summary is read only by the agent that wrote it. A context item is never edited: a change is a new item that replaces the old one.
declared-context.why: The user and the reader of an agent's definition can see exactly what it reads, and loading less keeps the prompt fast.
declared-context.tradeoff: An agent that needs a new kind needs its declaration changed, and a new kind is a migration.

whole-items.title: Loading chooses whole items, in the declared order, within a character limit
whole-items.decision: Kinds load in the order the agent declares them, newest first within a kind, whole items only; an item that doesn't fit what is left of the limit is skipped and reported.
whole-items.why: The simplest rule a reader of the agent's definition can predict, and characters need no tokenizer per model.
whole-items.tradeoff: Characters only approximate tokens, and an old item never loads while newer ones fill the limit.

load-with-fakes.title: Load simulated locally with fakes
load-with-fakes.decision: Load tests run locally against fakes for the model and speech, so simulating 1,000 users costs nothing.
load-with-fakes.why: Shows where voice-guide's own code and database stop keeping up, with no provider bill.
load-with-fakes.tradeoff: Provider limits and real latencies are not tested.

session-summary.title: A session's summary: written by its agent's own model, with the agent's instruction, read back only by that agent
session-summary.decision: When a session ends, a background job asks the session's model, outside any session, for what it learned, as the agent's summary instruction says, and saves it through user context. Only that agent's next session with the user loads it, the latest first, dated; the session's product hears it with the session's delivery.
session-summary.why: What is worth remembering differs per agent, and the agent that wrote the summary is the one that knows what it is for.
session-summary.tradeoff: The summary arrives a few seconds after the end, so a session started at once may open without it; each summary is a billed model call.

product-keys.title: A product's server starts each session with its key; the user's browser holds only what voice-guide signed
product-keys.decision: A product's server proves its workspace with a product key, kept only as its SHA-256, and starts each session itself for the user it names by its own stable ID. The start answers with a ticket the browser holds for that one session: signed by voice-guide, working until the session ends or for four hours at most.
product-keys.why: Every start passes the product's server, so it decides who may start a session and what the agent is told, and its key never reaches a browser; a copy of the database holds only hashes. A product signing its own tokens would need its key kept readable, and a public key in the page can be copied by anyone.
product-keys.tradeoff: The product needs a server and calls voice-guide before each session; a stolen ticket works in its one session until the product ends it with its key or four hours pass; rotating the signing key drops every user.

session-webhook.title: A product's server hears each ended session at its webhook: signed, after the summary, the same delivery ID on every attempt
session-webhook.decision: Once a session ends and its summary job has settled, a job on a runner of its own posts the session, its turns as heard and its summary to the workspace's webhook, signed by the core with HMAC-SHA256 under a per-workspace secret, one delivery ID on every attempt; any answer but 2xx is tried again for about 15 hours, and 410 Gone stops the webhook.
session-webhook.why: The product hears what each session covered without polling, verifies it with the libraries the Standard Webhooks shape already has, and drops a repeat by its ID.
session-webhook.tradeoff: The secret is kept readable, so a copy of the database could forge deliveries to that product; a delivery arrives after the summary, with no ceiling while the summary waits.

any-origin.title: A session's routes and the drop-in client answer pages on any site; a product's routes answer none
any-origin.decision: A session's routes answer a page on any origin, with no cookies, and the router answers their preflight from the route alone; a product's routes send no CORS headers and refuse their preflight, and a product key sent with an Origin header is refused unread. voice serves the drop-in client at /client/voice-guide.js, with no credential, to any site.
any-origin.why: The ticket in the Authorization header is a session route's only credential and no cookie is ever read, so a page on another site gains nothing its ticket doesn't give; with a product's routes closed to pages, its key never leaves its server.
any-origin.tradeoff: Any page may send requests, each still needing its ticket; a session's first turn, audio offer and end each wait for a preflight; a product can't end a session from its page; an allowlist of a product's sites waits for dashboards.

views.title: System
views.lead: A user's browser talks to one Go service, voice. Speech-to-text, text-to-speech and the model each run in their own process behind it, and PostgreSQL holds everything that must survive. Outside voice-guide's own containers, voice reaches only the model provider and, once a session has ended, the product's server.
views.start:
This is voice-guide from the outside: the user's browser, the voice service, what runs behind it and who calls it.
Start with a walk-through on the right to watch a turn or a session go by, or double-click a card to open it.

steps.caption: You speak; the browser streams your microphone to voice over WebRTC, and speech detection notices your words begin
voice streams the utterance to the speech-to-text service; the rough text that comes back while you talk shows on the page
You stop talking; after a 0.2 s pause voice asks for the final text and, at the same time, asks the end-of-turn check whether you've finished, from your last 8 s
With the final text in and the end-of-turn check saying you've finished, or 3 s of quiet, voice reads the saved turns, asks the model service, and saves your words
The model service hands the prompt to the model provider, through its API or a session process, and streams the reply back as JSON lines, a few words at a time
voice shows the reply on the page and has the text-to-speech service speak it a phrase at a time, the first short, playing it to you over WebRTC in 20 ms packets
Once the model has finished and the first audio has reached you, voice saves the reply with the turn; the stage times follow when it has all played
The product's server lists its agents with its product key; voice finds the workspace by the key's hash and answers with each agent's newest version
The product's server starts a session with one agent, naming the user by its user reference and sending the session context the agent declares
voice loads what the agent may know about the user, then saves the session on the agent's newest version, adding the user with their first session
voice answers with the session and a ticket that works only in this session, for at most four hours; the product key stays on the server
The product's server hands the session and ticket to its page: voice-guide's own browser page, or a product's page passing them to the drop-in client's join()
The page sends an audio offer with the ticket, a product's page loading the drop-in client from voice first; voice checks the session is live and answers
The audio connection opens; if the agent speaks first, the page asks for its opening on the data channel, and you hear the greeting
You press End: the page hangs up its audio connection first, so a reply still playing is saved cut where you stopped hearing it, then ends the session
Or the product's server ends it with its product key, or voice ends it after five minutes with no turn and none of your speech
voice marks the session ended, once, and in the same write queues its summary job and, if the workspace has a webhook, a delivery job to follow it
A runner claims the summary job: voice reads the turns as you heard them and asks the model for notes, as the agent's summary instruction says
voice saves the notes as a session summary, which only this agent's next session with you loads
Once the summary job is done or has failed for good, the delivery job posts the session, its turns and summary, signed, to the product's webhook
A 2xx answer delivers it; any other but 410 Gone is tried again, eight attempts over about 15 hours, with the same delivery ID
You type and send; the page puts your words on the audio connection's data channel, or posts them with the ticket when there is no audio connection
voice reads the session's saved turns, asks the model service for a reply, and saves your words as a turn in flight while the model starts
The model's reply streams back through the model service, and voice passes the text on as it comes: on the data channel, or as server-sent events
On an audio connection the reply is spoken too: the text-to-speech service speaks it a phrase at a time, and voice plays it to you over WebRTC
Once the model has finished, voice saves the reply with the turn, then its stage times

nodes.name: Product's server
nodes.tech: stand-in: web dev server, the demo job board, the drive-session skill
nodes.summary: Keeps the product key and starts each session for its user; hears each ended session at its webhook.
nodes.description: Whoever embeds voice-guide runs a server that keeps its product key and starts each session itself: it names the agent, its user by its own stable ID (a user reference, never a name or an email address) and the session context it already knows, so it decides who may start a session and what the agent is told. It hands the browser the ticket each start answers with, for that one session, never the key. Keys are made, listed and revoked by cmd/productkey (scripts/product-key.sh); the seed registers the development key in .env as VOICE_DEV_PRODUCT_KEY. In development the web page's Vite dev server plays this part: /product/agents lists the agents with the key, and /product/start starts the session with the key, the placeholder user's reference and the session context the agent declares, the invented files in seed/, then hands the page the session and its ticket; .claude/skills/drive-session/start-session.sh does the same and keeps the ticket under .tickets/ for .claude/skills/drive-session/turn.sh and .claude/skills/drive-session/end-session.sh. Once a session has ended, it hears of it at its webhook, set with cmd/webhook (scripts/webhook.sh): voice posts the session, its turns as the user heard them and its summary, signed with the webhook's secret, and keeps one delivery ID on every attempt so the product drops a repeat.
nodes.why: Every session starts at the product's server, so it decides who may talk to its agents and what they are told, and its product key never reaches a browser.

nodes.name: Browser page
nodes.summary: Where the user talks or types to an agent: microphone in, agent audio out, transcript and timings.
nodes.description: The page a user talks to an agent on. It lists the agents and starts a session through the product's server, which hands it the session and its ticket, then holds it with the same code as the drop-in client (web/src/client/joined.ts), drawn in React. The session's audio connection opens with one request: the microphone goes in with the browser's echo cancellation on, the agent's audio comes back, and a data channel carries typed turns and every message about a turn. Without a microphone, the user types. It times what the user feels: from send to the reply's first text and first sound, and how soon an interrupted reply went quiet.
nodes.why: It calls the same API any product would, so the API never drifts toward one screen.

nodes.name: Product's page
nodes.summary: A product's page holding <voice-guide-session>: joined with a session's ticket, it talks, types and ends.
nodes.description: Where a product puts an agent in front of its users: a page on the product's own site, which loads the drop-in client from voice at /client/voice-guide.js and puts a <voice-guide-session> element on it. The element holds the session with the same code as the web page, without React (npm run build:client writes web/dist-client/). The page hands it the session ID and ticket its server's start answered with by join({ session, ticket }), never an attribute, which session-replay scripts copy; it never holds a product key or starts a session. It opens the session's audio connection at once, adds the microphone once allowed, asks for the agent's opening once the browser plays the agent (over HTTP if the audio connection fails), streams the transcript, offers typing, Mute and End, reconnects with the same ticket, and fires voice-guide-ended and voice-guide-error. Its requests to voice are cross-origin, which a session's routes answer for any site; a closed shadow root keeps the product's styles and scripts out.
nodes.why: The drop-in client runs in the product's own page, not a frame, so the microphone prompt names the product's site and the ticket goes through join(), never an attribute.

nodes.name: voice
nodes.summary: One Go service: conversation, speech, user context and agents behind one router checking every credential.
nodes.description: One Go program holding four fenced modules: conversation and speech (together, voice, the part that gives an agent a voice), user context and agents, behind one router that checks every request's product key or ticket. It holds no conversation in memory between requests, so any instance serves any turn; a session's audio connection lives on the instance that answered it. Every instance also runs background jobs from one queue in PostgreSQL, such as a session's summary once it ends.
nodes.why: One service with fenced modules is the simplest to build, run and measure; it holds no conversation in memory, so more copies serve more users.

nodes.name: Model service
nodes.tech: TypeScript · Claude API SDK · Claude Agent SDK
nodes.summary: One request per reply, answered as JSON lines; Claude through its API or a subscription, or a fake.
nodes.description: A small TypeScript service on this machine (port 8091 unless set) that reaches the model for voice. Each reply is one POST /v1/replies, answered by one JSON event per line: text as it arrives, then done with the provider, model, usage and timing, or an error naming its kind and never the provider's message. Its provider is a setting: claude-api, Claude through the provider's Messages API on an API key that only this service reads, keeping nothing between replies, with the layers and the conversation marked for the provider's cache; claude-subscription, Claude through the Claude Agent SDK on the developer's login, keeping one Claude Code process per session between turns as a disposable cache, rebuilt from the whole conversation whenever it no longer matches; or fake, set text at a set pace for load tests. An ask outside any session, such as a session's summary, keeps nothing and runs one at a time within the cap, so live turns keep the other places.
nodes.why: No route from Go reaches the model on a subscription, so a small TypeScript service does, behind a swap point any model can replace.

nodes.name: Speech-to-text service
nodes.summary: Turns streamed speech into rough, then final text, and judges from the audio whether the user has finished.
nodes.description: A small Python service (aiohttp, port 8092, built by compose in the stt profile) with two endpoints. /v1/realtime speaks the part of OpenAI's realtime transcription API voice uses: Moonshine's streaming English model turns 24 kHz PCM16 into rough text while the user speaks, then one final text per committed utterance. POST /v1/turn/check runs Smart Turn on up to the last 8 s of 16 kHz audio and answers whether the user has finished. Moonshine's size is chosen when the image is built.
nodes.why: Its speech-to-text model ships for Python and sends text while you talk; the service speaks a standard realtime API, so another can swap in by setting.

nodes.name: Text-to-speech service
nodes.summary: Text-to-speech: speaks each phrase of the reply as streamed Ogg Opus.
nodes.description: By default Kokoro-FastAPI on the CPU, a pinned third-party image that compose starts in the tts profile (port 8880); KOKORO=mlx runs it natively on a Mac instead: the same model and voice through Apple's MLX, in a small server of ours with the same API. voice asks it for one phrase at a time at POST /v1/audio/speech, with the Opus format and streaming on, and unwraps the Ogg pages into 20 ms Opus packets itself. Its errors reach voice's logs as a status only, since its reasons can quote what the user said.
nodes.why: Free and natural-sounding on a CPU, and its Opus goes straight to the browser, so voice needs no audio encoder.

nodes.name: PostgreSQL 18
nodes.summary: Everything that must survive: sessions, turns, timings, agent versions, context items, keys, webhooks.
nodes.description: PostgreSQL 18 in compose, the only store. Conversation's tables (workspaces, users, user_references, sessions, turns, turn_stages, webhooks, whose secret is kept readable since signing needs it) and product_keys, which keeps only each key's hash, sit in the default schema; agents keeps agent.agents and agent.agent_versions and user context keeps user_context.context_items in schemas of their own. Migrations in migrations/ are applied by cmd/migrate, never by the service, and agent versions are written only by cmd/publish.
nodes.why: One relational store until a measured need for another, with version 18 for native UUIDv7 IDs.

nodes.name: Model provider
nodes.summary: The model provider, outside voice-guide's containers, reached through its API or the developer's subscription.
nodes.description: The model provider. The model service reaches it through its Messages API, billed per token to an API key, or through the Claude Agent SDK, which runs Claude Code on the developer's personal subscription login: for development only, since the API replaces it before anyone else uses voice-guide. Which model answers is the one the agent file names with model:, else voice's VOICE_MODEL (Sonnet 5.5 unless set), and is sent with every request.
nodes.why: Which model answers, and the route to it, are settings; the model is recorded with every turn.

edges.send: agents · the session and its ticket
edges.detail: A product's server starts the session and hands the browser its ID and ticket, which works only in that session, until it ends or for four hours, and the browser reuses for every request and audio reconnect, with no refresh. The development page asks the dev server's /product/agents and /product/start, which sends the placeholder user's reference and resume to voice; no ticket or key is ever built into the page.

edges.send: the session and its ticket, for join()
edges.detail: The product's server starts the session with its key and hands its own page the session's ID and ticket, never the key; the page passes them to the element's join(). The element tells the page when the session is over, with the reason, and the refusal that made it unusable, never the ticket.

edges.send: product key · user's ID · agent · context · end
edges.back: agents · the session and its ticket
edges.detail: GET /v1/agents, POST /v1/sessions and POST /v1/sessions/{id}/end, which ends any session of the product's workspace, as when a ticket was stolen, with 'Authorization: Bearer' and the product key; the start names its user by the product's own stable ID ('user'), added with their first session. The start answers with the session and a ticket for it, fresh on a repeat whose reply was lost, in a reply no cache keeps; a ticket sent here is refused (401). A key sent with an Origin header, as only a page sends, is refused unread (401). A key revoked, unknown or malformed is refused (401); one the database can't check is a 503, so the product retries.

edges.back: 2xx, or a status to retry or stop
edges.detail: A POST of JSON to the workspace's webhook URL with webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature (v1, an HMAC-SHA256 of the ID, the time and the body under the webhook's secret), run as a background job once the session's summary job has settled. 2xx delivers it; 408, 429, 5xx and no answer within 15 s are tried again over about 15 hours; 410 Gone stops deliveries until the URL is set again; any other answer, a redirect included, which isn't followed, fails it.

edges.send: end session · typed turns · audio offer
edges.detail: POST /v1/sessions/{id}/turns, its reply streamed back as text events, then done or lost; POST /v1/sessions/{id}/end; POST /v1/sessions/{id}/audio with the SDP offer, answered 201 with the SDP answer and the connection's own address, which DELETE ends. Every request carries 'Authorization: Bearer' and the session's ticket, which reaches only its own session's routes (another session's is answered 404, one past four hours 401 of type ticket-expired); errors are problem details. The page reaches voice through its dev server's /v1 proxy, on one origin.

edges.back: the drop-in client · JSON · events · SDP answer
edges.detail: GET /client/voice-guide.js, answered as text/javascript to any origin, no-cache with a tag from its content, so every load asks and gets 304 while the build is unchanged; 404 until it is built. Then the session's routes, with the ticket, from the product's own origin: the router answers each route's preflight itself (204, its method, Authorization and Content-Type, kept two hours) with no handler run, and every answer, refusals included, allows any origin and lets the page read Location and Retry-After. A preflight for a product's route is refused (405).

edges.back: agent audio (Opus) · hearing, text, done, spoken
edges.detail: Media flows straight to the server that answered the offer, on its private addresses: the microphone with echo cancellation on, decoded in Go to 16 kHz, and the agent's 20 ms Opus packets paced in real time. The data channel carries JSON both ways in order: the page sends turn, the user's words or, once the connection opens, the agent's opening; voice sends hearing, text, done, lost, refused, failed, spoken, interrupted, talking_on and closing.

edges.send: model, session, stable layers, conversation, new words
edges.back: text …, then done (usage, timing) or error
edges.detail: One POST /v1/replies per reply. A session's summary is the same request with no session, so the model service keeps nothing for it.

/v1/realtime?intent=transcription, a transcription session with no turn detection, so voice decides when each utterance ends: audio appended as base64, then committed or cleared. One connection per audio connection, opened at its first speech; speech's 16 kHz audio is resampled to 24 kHz on the way.

edges.send: last 8 s of audio (16 kHz L16)
edges.detail: POST /v1/turn/check after each 0.2 s pause, with a one-second deadline, so the maximum wait decides when the check can't.

edges.send: one phrase of the reply, the voice
edges.detail: POST /v1/audio/speech with model kokoro, the phrase as input, the voice (af_heart unless set), response_format opus and stream on. One phrase at a time, the next asked for once the one before is made; a phrase whose first audio hasn't come within 5 s fails.

edges.send: sessions, turns, timings, versions, context, jobs, keys
edges.detail: Over a pgx pool, with queries sqlc generated from SQL. Only each module's store adapter touches the database, and every query names the workspace, except the system's sweeps and the product key check, which finds a key by its hash across workspaces.

On the API route, one streamed request per reply carries everything, with the agent's layer, the session's layers and the conversation so far marked for the provider's cache; the SDK's retries are off and its timeout is the reply's deadline. On the subscription route, the Claude Agent SDK runs a Claude Code process per session, kept between turns, on the developer's login; Claude Code's own retries and compaction are off, and it gets only the environment variables it needs, so the service's secrets never reach it.

views.title: Inside voice
views.lead: Four modules with walls between them, checked on every push. Speech calls conversation and never the other way round; conversation calls user context's service and agents' catalog directly. The router, the ticket check, product keys, the caller and the job runner sit outside the modules and import none of them: each module's HTTP adapter plugs into the one router, and cmd/voice hands the runner each kind of job's handler.

steps.caption: You speak; your microphone reaches speech over WebRTC, decoded to 16 kHz, and speech detection notices your words begin
speech streams the utterance to the speech-to-text service over a WebSocket and tells the page the rough text as it comes back
You stop talking; after 0.2 s speech asks for the final text and, at once, sends your last 8 s to the end-of-turn check, waiting a second at most
Once you've finished, speech hands conversation the turn, which builds the prompt from the agent version, the loaded context items and the saved turns
conversation asks the model service for a reply, saves your words as a turn in flight, and passes the reply's text back to speech as it streams
speech shows the text on the page and has the text-to-speech service speak it a phrase at a time, playing the Ogg Opus to you as 20 ms packets
Once the model has finished and the first audio has reached you, speech has conversation save the reply; the stage times follow when it has all played
The product's server calls the router with its product key; product keys find the workspace by the key's SHA-256, never keeping the key itself
The router hands conversation the caller, the product's server; conversation checks the agent is the workspace's and the session context matches its version
user context loads what the agent may know about the user, within a limit; conversation saves the session with those items' IDs
The router has tickets sign an HS256 ticket for this session alone, and answers the product's server with the session and the ticket
The page gets the session and ticket from its server; a product's page loads the drop-in client from the router and joins with them
For the audio offer, tickets verify the ticket is this session's; the router hands speech the caller, and speech checks with conversation that the session is live
speech answers the offer, and the audio connection opens straight to it: your microphone in, the agent's audio and the data channel out
You press End: the page first hangs up its audio connection, and speech has conversation save a reply still playing cut where you stopped hearing it
Then the page ends the session with its ticket, accepted up to 15 minutes past its four hours, and the router hands that to conversation
Or the product's server ends it with its product key, or cmd/voice's once-a-minute sweep ends it after five minutes with no turn and no speech
conversation marks the session ended, once, and in the same write queues a summary job and, if the workspace has a webhook, a delivery job that waits on it
The summaries' runner, started by cmd/voice, claims the job under a lease and calls conversation's Summarize
conversation reads the agent's summary instruction, asks the model service for notes on the turns as you heard them, and has user context save the summary
Then the deliveries' runner calls Deliver: conversation reads back the summary, signs the session with its turns, and posts it to the product's webhook

nodes.name: cmd/voice
nodes.summary: Reads settings, builds the adapters, wires the modules; ends idle sessions and runs background jobs.
nodes.description: The service's entry point and the only code that imports every module. It reads its settings from the environment, refusing unusable ones at start, opens the database pool, builds each adapter its settings choose (Kokoro or the fake text-to-speech, Silero or the fake speech detection), wires them into conversation and speech, registers both HTTP adapters on the router, points it at the drop-in client's folder (VOICE_CLIENT_DIR, web/dist-client unless set) and serves it. A sweeper goroutine ends idle sessions once a minute. Stopping ends every audio connection and waits for the turns in flight to be saved. It also starts two job runners, each claiming only its own kinds: one for summaries, one at a time, and one for deliveries to products' servers, four at a time, and deletes jobs done a week ago once an hour.
nodes.why: Only programs in cmd/ wire modules together, so each module's core never chooses its own adapters.

nodes.name: Router
nodes.summary: The public API's one router: every route behind a key or ticket check, open to any site where tickets go.
nodes.description: The public API's one router, the same an outside product calls and voice-guide's own page uses. Each module's HTTP adapter registers its routes here, the only way to add one: HandleProduct for a route a product's server calls, which takes its product key and refuses a ticket, and Handle for a route in one session, which the browser calls with that session's ticket: a ticket for another session is answered 404, as a session that doesn't exist, one past its four hours 401 of type ticket-expired, and a key is refused without being read. HandleSessionEnd, for the session's end, takes the ticket up to 15 minutes past its four hours too, and the product's key as well. Each puts the route behind the check and a deadline of its own, and a key's caller is marked a product, naming the workspace and no user. It mints the ticket a start answers with. Every error, including unknown paths and wrong methods, is an RFC 9457 problem details document. The routes Handle and HandleSessionEnd register answer a page on any origin, and the router answers their preflight from the route alone, with no handler run and no credential read; HandleProduct's routes send no CORS headers and their preflight is refused. A product key sent with an Origin header is refused before it is read, on every route. Without a credential it serves only those preflights and the drop-in client, from the folder cmd/voice gives it, read at each request.
nodes.why: One router checks every credential in one place, so no module's routes can skip the check.

nodes.name: Tickets
nodes.summary: Makes and checks the HS256 tickets that work in one session.
nodes.description: Makes and checks what voice-guide signs for the browser, with no database read: a ticket naming the session's workspace, its user and the session itself, living at most four hours from its session's start, however late it was minted. It checks the signature, the algorithm and the times, refuses a credential with no session, ignores a claim it doesn't read, and reports one past its four hours apart, so the page can say the session has expired. VerifyToEnd takes a ticket up to 15 minutes past its four hours, for ending its session. A Ticket prints, logs and encodes redacted.
nodes.why: The browser holds only what voice-guide signed, for one session, so a copied ticket opens nothing else.

nodes.name: Caller
nodes.summary: Who calls: workspace, user and the session a ticket allows, or a product's server.
nodes.description: Says who a request comes from (its workspace, its user and the one session its ticket works in, or a product's server, proven by its key, naming its workspace and no user) and imports nothing of voice-guide's, so the router, the ticket check, conversation and speech all name a caller without the router or the tickets importing a module.
nodes.why: A plain type every part may import, so the caller crosses module walls without a module importing another.

nodes.name: Product keys
nodes.summary: Makes product keys and checks one by its SHA-256 across workspaces; the key itself is never kept.
nodes.description: Makes a product key (vgk_ and 256 random bits), keeping only its SHA-256 and first 12 characters, checks one by finding its hash among the working keys of every workspace, and lists and revokes a workspace's keys. A key is held in a type that prints, logs and encodes redacted. Like the ticket check it imports no module, so the router checks keys without reaching into one; its store is an adapter of its own.
nodes.why: Only each key's hash is kept, so a copy of the database can't be used to act for a workspace.

nodes.name: conversation
nodes.summary: Sessions and their turns, in text: the prompt, the model's reply, what was said; a summary, then a delivery.
nodes.description: Runs sessions and their turns in text: it builds each turn's layered prompt, asks the model, streams the reply and records what was said and how long each stage took. Typed and spoken words take the same path, so a product without audio uses it unchanged. When a session ends, it queues the session's summary, then writes it as a background job and saves it through user context. When the workspace has a webhook, another job, queued with the end, waits for the summary's, then posts the session to the product's server, signed.
nodes.why: Text only, whether the words were typed or spoken, so speech can be swapped or left out without touching it.

nodes.name: speech
nodes.summary: The audio connection: hears the user's words, speaks the reply, cuts in, says how much was heard.
nodes.description: Gives replies a sound and the user's speech words: it holds each session's audio connection, notices speech, streams it to speech-to-text, asks whether the user has finished, speaks the reply phrase by phrase and works out how much of it was heard when the user cuts in. Every turn it takes goes to conversation.
nodes.why: Speech calls conversation and never the reverse, so conversation stays text-only.

nodes.name: user context
nodes.summary: Loads what an agent may know about the user, within a limit; saves each session's summary.
nodes.description: Loads what an agent may know about the user from earlier conversations: only the kinds the agent declares, whole items, newest first, within a character limit voice sends. It keeps its own tables and imports none of the other modules. It saves a session's summary once per session, read back only by the agent that wrote it.
nodes.why: It imports no other module and keeps its own tables, so what an agent may know about a user is decided in one place.

nodes.name: agents
nodes.summary: Agent definitions and their versions; the catalog serves each workspace's newest and exact ones.
nodes.description: Holds agent definitions and their published versions: persona, the context kinds each reads, the session context it expects, its summary instruction and whether it speaks first. The catalog reads the newest versions on every request and keeps exact versions in memory once read. Versions are written only by cmd/publish, from agents/<name>.md.
nodes.why: Versions never change once saved, so any instance finds the exact version a session started on, even mid-deploy.

nodes.name: Job runner
nodes.summary: Runs background work from one queue: claims its own kinds, a lease, retries with growing waits.
nodes.description: Runs work too slow for a request. A module queues a job by inserting its row, its kind and its inputs, in the same write that calls for it; each runner claims the job due soonest of the kinds it has handlers for, holds it for a lease, and runs it with its kind's handler, so an instance runs a runner per group of kinds and a slow group holds up no other. A failed run waits and runs again, longer each time, until the job is done or out of attempts; a run that finds what it needs busy is let go without counting. It imports no module: cmd/voice hands it each kind's handler.
nodes.why: One queue keeps claiming, the lease and retries written and tested once, and slow work never runs inside a request.

nodes.name: Product's server
nodes.summary: Lists agents, starts and ends sessions with its key; hears each ended session at its webhook.

nodes.name: Browser page
nodes.summary: HTTP through the dev server's proxy; WebRTC straight to this server.

nodes.name: Product's page
nodes.summary: Loads the drop-in client; calls a session's routes from its own site.

nodes.name: Model service
nodes.summary: Reaches the model.

nodes.name: Speech-to-text
nodes.summary: Speech to text and the end-of-turn check.

nodes.name: Text-to-speech
nodes.summary: Speaks each phrase of the reply.

nodes.name: PostgreSQL 18
nodes.summary: Each module's own tables; the jobs queue.

edges.send: agents · start, end a session, with the product key
edges.back: agents · the session and its ticket · problem details
edges.detail: GET /v1/agents and POST /v1/sessions, the routes registered through HandleProduct; the start names the user by the product's own stable ID.

edges.send: session routes with the session's ticket
edges.detail: Turns, the end and the audio connection, each in one session. Every route sits behind the router's check: a ticket reaches only its own session's routes, and a request without a valid ticket never reaches a module.

edges.send: the drop-in client · session routes, cross-origin
edges.detail: GET /client/voice-guide.js, served by the router with no credential to any site; then preflights, which the router answers from the route alone, and the session's routes with its ticket, each answer allowing any origin.

edges.back: the caller, refused, or a ticket
edges.detail: Checked on every request before the route's handler runs, with no database read, so any instance checks any request; a start's reply carries a ticket the router mints for the session.

Only on the routes a product's server calls; a key sent where the browser's ticket belongs, or sent from a page with an Origin header, is refused unread. A key revoked, unknown or malformed is refused (401); one the database can't check is a 503, never a 401.
A verified ticket becomes an access.Caller, handed to the route's handler; conversation and speech take it with every call.

conversation's HTTP adapter registers GET /v1/agents and POST /v1/sessions through HandleProduct (a product's key) and POST /v1/sessions/{id}/turns and POST /v1/sessions/{id}/end through Handle (a ticket).
speech's HTTP adapter registers POST /v1/sessions/{id}/audio and DELETE /v1/sessions/{id}/audio/{conn}, the shape WHIP gives them.
The audio connection the offer set up: Opus both ways and the data channel's JSON messages.
The sweeper ends every session idle for five minutes in one statement; a failed sweep is logged and tried again a minute later.

edges.send: words heard · how much of the reply was heard
edges.back: the reply's text as it streams
edges.detail: speech calls conversation's service directly: Session to check a session before an offer, TakeTurn for every typed or spoken turn, Interrupted to save a cut reply as far as it was heard, TakeBack and Settle for talking on, Active to mark the user's speech (as often as SessionIdle allows), RecordTiming once a turn is saved. conversation never imports speech.

edges.send: Load · Items by ID · SaveSummary · SessionSummary
edges.detail: At a session's start, Load with the kinds the agent version declares and the character limit; on each turn, Items reads the loaded items back by ID, in the order loaded. Through user context's service only, never its store. Once a session ends, its summary job saves the summary through SaveSummary. A delivery reads the session's summary as it stands through SessionSummary.
Available lists the workspace's newest versions to start a session with; Version reads the exact version a running session started on, for its prompt.
Through conversation's model adapter.
Through conversation's webhook adapter, as a background job once the session's summary job has settled.
Through speech's speech-to-text adapter (WebSocket) and its end-of-turn adapter (HTTP).

edges.send: the reply, a phrase at a time
edges.detail: Through speech's text-to-speech adapter.

A product's new user and their reference are added in the same write as their first session. Ending a session, or the idle sweep, inserts its summary job in the same statement, so the job exists exactly when the end commits, and, for a workspace with a webhook not stopped, its delivery job, waiting on the summary's.

edges.send: product_keys: add, find by hash, list, revoke, count
edges.detail: Finding a key by its hash looks across workspaces, since the key is what names the workspace; every other query names the workspace.

edges.send: two runners: summaries, deliveries · Run · Prune
edges.detail: cmd/voice builds a runner for summaries, one worker, and one for deliveries, four workers and eight attempts, over its PostgreSQL store, each claiming only the kinds it has a handler for, runs both until voice stops; each prunes its own kinds' jobs done a week ago every hour.

The summary's handler calls conversation's Summarize; a model service with no place for it is busy, so the job is let go without using a run. The delivery's handler calls Deliver; an answer posting again wouldn't change fails the job at once.

edges.send: jobs: claim, done, retry, release, fail, prune
edges.detail: Claiming takes the job due soonest that no run holds, skipping locked rows, so two instances never take the same job.

views.title: conversation
views.lead: Hexagonal: the core holds the rules and declares its ports, Sessions, Turns, Model, Webhooks and Poster, as small interfaces. The HTTP adapter and speech call the core; the stores, the model client and the webhook poster implement its ports. cmd/voice wires the PostgreSQL stores, the HTTP model client and the HTTP poster in.

steps.caption: Your page posts your words with its ticket; the router checks the ticket is for this session and hands the request, with the caller, to the http adapter
The adapter calls TakeTurn, which checks your words and screen input against their limits and reads the session, refusing one that has ended
It reads the session's agent version, the context items the session loaded and the turns saved so far, then renders the layered prompt, stable layers first
The model is asked first: the HTTP model client posts the prompt to the model service, whose events come back line by line
Meanwhile the turn is saved in flight as the session's next, with your words; the reply's text waits until that save is done
Each piece of the reply goes back to your page as a server-sent text event the moment it arrives
When the reply ends, the turn is saved answered, or lost if the model failed; your page gets done, then the turn's stage times are saved
The product's server posts the agent, a request ID, its user reference and any session context; the router checks its product key
StartSession takes the newest version of each of the workspace's agents from the catalog, and refuses an agent not among them
It finds the user the reference names, or makes a new user ID; the same request sent again gets back the session it started
If the agent version reads context kinds, user context loads the user's items within the character limit; the session keeps their IDs
The session is saved with its agent version, the context item IDs and the session context, a new user added in the same write
The http adapter answers 201 with the session and a ticket that lets the user's browser into this session only
If the agent speaks first, the user's page then asks for the opening on its audio connection: a first turn with no words, a fixed cue in their place
The session is ended through the API; the same write queues its summary job and, if the workspace's webhook isn't stopped, a delivery job after it
The job runner calls Summarize, which reads the ended session and its turns; a turn still in flight sends the job back to run again
If the user said anything and the agent version has a summary instruction, the model writes notes from the transcript as the user heard it, outside any session
The summary, at most 2,000 characters, is saved through user context, for the agent to read in its next session with this user
Once the summary job is done or has failed for good, the runner calls Deliver, which reads the workspace's webhook as it is now: its URL and secret
It builds the delivery from the session, the user reference, the turns as the user heard them, and the summary, if one was written
It signs the body with the secret and posts it to the product's server, following no redirects: 2xx delivers it, 410 Gone stops the webhook, anything else is tried again

nodes.name: Service
nodes.summary: Use cases: agents, start and end sessions, take a turn, save a cut, take one back, summarize an ended session.
nodes.description: conversation's use cases, called by its HTTP adapter and by speech once they have proven who the caller is. Starting a session finds the user a product's server names by its own stable ID, or adds them with their first session, checks the session context against the agent version and loads user context; taking a turn keeps one in flight per session, saves the user's words while the model starts, streams the reply and saves how it ended, and a turn is saved before the next prompt is built; an agent that opens takes its opening only as the session's first turn, a fixed cue in the user's place. It also saves a cut reply as far as it was heard, settles or takes back a spoken turn, ends a session, and ends idle ones. Summarize, run as a background job once a session ends, asks the session's model outside any session for what it learned, as the agent's summary instruction says, from the conversation as the user heard it, waits while a turn is still in flight, and saves the summary through user context once per session.
nodes.why: The database is the conversation's source of truth, so any instance can take any turn.

nodes.name: Prompt
nodes.summary: Renders the layered prompt from what the session recorded, stable layers first.
nodes.description: Domain logic, called directly rather than through a port: one function renders the prompt from what the session recorded, so every turn and every instance produces the same bytes. The agent's persona and the session's context form the stable layers; the conversation follows, with a cut reply only as far as it was heard, then the screen input and the new words.
nodes.why: One function renders every turn's prompt, stable layers first, so the model's cache is hit and every instance sends the same bytes.

nodes.name: Deliveries
nodes.summary: Signs each ended session, as heard, and posts it to its webhook; sets the URL and makes the secret.
nodes.description: Deliver, run as a background job once the session's summary job has settled, builds the body at its run from the session, the product's reference for the user, the turns as the user heard them and the summary, the earliest turns left out past 256 KiB, then signs it: webhook-id, the delivery's one ID; webhook-timestamp, the attempt's time by its clock; webhook-signature, v1 and the HMAC-SHA256 of the two and the body under the secret the webhook has at this attempt. 2xx delivers it; 410 Gone stops the webhook, and a delivery to a stopped webhook is ErrWebhookStopped, naming its session; any other answer, or none, is tried again. SetWebhook takes an https URL, or http on this machine, and makes the secret, whsec_ and 32 random bytes, the first time only; RotateWebhookSecret replaces it. A WebhookSecret prints, logs and encodes redacted.
nodes.why: The core signs each delivery with HMAC-SHA256 in the Standard Webhooks shape, so a product's server verifies it with libraries it already has.

nodes.name: Sessions
nodes.summary: Where sessions are kept.
nodes.description: The port for keeping sessions: find one by its request ID or ID within the caller's workspace, or by ID in a product's workspace, whichever user's, find the user a product names by reference, and the reference a user is named by, start one once per request ID, adding a product's new user and their reference in the same write, end one keeping the first end time and queuing its summary job, and its delivery job for a workspace with a webhook, in the same write, mark it active, and end every idle one in a single sweep.

nodes.name: Turns
nodes.summary: Where turns and their stage times are kept, read by session in order.
nodes.description: The port for turns, kept behind their own interface so they can move to another store if PostgreSQL stops keeping up. Start saves a turn in flight as the session's next, refusing a second in flight, a repeated request ID, or an opening once the session has a turn; Finish, Cut and Remove settle it; Finished reads the session's finished turns in order for the prompt; InFlight tells a summary whether a turn is still under way, and CutOff saves one left in flight past the deadline as lost; RecordStages writes each stage's time.
nodes.why: Every turn records how long each stage took, so 'faster' can be measured stage by stage.

nodes.name: Model
nodes.summary: Asks for one reply and streams its events back.
nodes.description: The model swap point: Reply asks for one reply to a layered prompt and streams its events on a channel, text as it arrives, then a final report (provider, model, usage, timing) or a failure of a known kind, closed soon after the context is cancelled.
nodes.why: Model vendors change fast in price, speed and terms; swapping one touches one adapter and one setting.

nodes.name: Webhooks
nodes.summary: Where each workspace's webhook is kept: its URL, its secret, whether it is stopped.
nodes.description: The port for keeping webhooks: read a workspace's; set its URL, starting deliveries again and keeping the secret it has, or the one given for a workspace with none; replace its secret; stop deliveries while the URL is still the one whose server answered 410 Gone.

nodes.name: Poster
nodes.summary: Posts one signed delivery to a product's server and says what it answered.
nodes.description: The port reaching products' servers: Post sends a delivery's body to its URL with the headers the core signed, and returns the HTTP status answered, or an error when no answer came within the deadline or the server couldn't be reached. It has one real implementation, so the network stays out of the core's tests; the core decides what each answer means.

nodes.name: http
nodes.summary: conversation's part of the API: agents, sessions, typed turns with the reply as server-sent events.
nodes.description: Inbound adapter: registers GET /v1/agents and POST /v1/sessions for a product's server, which calls with its key and names the user by its own stable ID, and gets back the session with a fresh ticket for it, minted by the router, and POST /v1/sessions/{id}/turns and POST /v1/sessions/{id}/end, which the product's server may also call with its key, turns requests into calls on the core, and streams a typed turn's reply as server-sent events: text, then done or lost. Refusals are problem details, with types of their own where a client must tell them apart; a user reference that can't be looked up is a 503.
nodes.why: The API is designed for products outside voice-guide; errors are standard problem details their tools already read.

nodes.name: store/postgres
nodes.summary: Sessions, turns, stage times and webhooks in PostgreSQL, through sqlc-generated queries.
nodes.description: Outbound adapter implementing Sessions, Turns and Webhooks over a pgx pool, with the queries in queries.sql and sqlc's generated db package. Every query filters by workspace except the idle-session sweep; a turn starting holds its session's row, so the end and the sweep see each other's writes. A product's new user and their reference go in with the first session, the reference first, so a start that finds it added by another adds no user of its own. Ending a session and the idle sweep insert the session's summary job into the jobs table in the same statement, and, for a workspace with a webhook not stopped, its delivery job, which waits on the summary's.

nodes.name: model/http
nodes.summary: Reaches the model service: one request per reply, events read line by line.
nodes.description: Outbound adapter implementing Model with the standard library alone: one POST /v1/replies per reply, its JSON-lines events read as they stream in, each line capped in size. A refusal at the service's own cap reads as busy, a provider overloaded as overloaded, a stream cut before its final event as unavailable; cancelling the turn closes the connection, which stops the provider.

nodes.name: webhook/http
nodes.summary: Posts each delivery, with the headers the core signed, to the product's server; no redirects.
nodes.description: Outbound adapter implementing Poster with the standard library alone: a POST of the JSON body with the headers given. Each attempt waits at most 15 s, 5 s of it to connect; a redirect is answered as it is, never followed; errors name no address, since a URL can hold a secret of the product's.

nodes.name: Router
nodes.summary: Key- and ticket-checked routes.

nodes.name: speech
nodes.summary: Calls the core for every typed or spoken turn on an audio connection.
