nodes.summary: Newest and exact agent versions.

nodes.name: user context · Service
nodes.summary: Declared context kinds; saves summaries and reads one back.

nodes.name: Job runner
nodes.summary: Runs the summary job, then the delivery job.

nodes.name: Product's server
nodes.summary: Hears each ended session at its webhook.

nodes.name: cmd/webhook
nodes.summary: Run by a member to set the URL, rotate the secret and show the webhook.

edges.detail: The router has checked the product key or the ticket, and hands each route the caller; a ticket reaches only its own session's turns and end.

edges.back: session · reply text, then the saved turn
edges.detail: TakeTurn takes a function the core calls with each piece of the reply as it arrives, which the adapter writes as a text event.
Also Session, to check a session before an audio offer, and RecordTiming once a turn is saved.

edges.send: start in flight, settle, read in order, in flight?
sqlc queries over pgx · summary and delivery jobs

edges.detail: Within 15 s an attempt, 5 s of it to connect; no redirect followed.
Called directly: domain logic of another module, not a port.
Called directly, through user context's service, never its store.
Through the handler cmd/voice registers for the session_summary kind.
Through the handler cmd/voice registers for the session_delivery kind on the deliveries' own runner, eight attempts; a delivery to a stopped webhook fails the job at once, logged with its session.
The secret is printed only when made; show reads the webhook through the Webhooks port and prints the URL alone.

edges.send: the webhook now · set · rotate · stop

edges.detail: Called directly, through user context's service, never its store.

views.title: speech
views.lead: Hexagonal, with a port for each speech stage: the audio transport, speech detection, speech-to-text, the end-of-turn check and text-to-speech. Only the adapter imports its vendor. The core takes every turn to conversation and never the other way round.

steps.caption: Your page sends its WebRTC offer; the service checks with conversation that the session is live, and the WebRTC transport answers, opening the audio connection
Your microphone arrives decoded to 16 kHz; the listener has speech detection judge each 32 ms frame, and the first frame judged speech opens an utterance
The utterance's audio, from 0.3 s before speech began, streams over a WebSocket at 24 kHz; rough text comes back and your page is shown it
You stop talking; once the quiet lasts the pause, the listener says so and the utterance is committed, asking for its final text
At the same moment the end-of-turn check is asked whether you've finished, from your last 8 s of audio, with a second to answer
With the final text in and the check saying you've finished, or the maximum wait up, your page is shown your words and the turn is taken in conversation
The service takes your spoken turn in conversation, held in flight, and the reply's text streams back piece by piece as the model writes it
Each piece goes at once to your page on the data channel and to text-to-speech, which never holds the text back
The text-to-speech adapter cuts the reply into phrases, a short one first, and asks the text-to-speech service for one phrase at a time, the next made while one plays
Each phrase's Ogg Opus is unwrapped into 20 ms packets marked with their phrase; the service plays one every 20 ms on the agent's track
When the reply's text is in and its first packet should have reached you, the turn is saved in conversation and your page is told done
Once all the audio has played, your page is told spoken and the turn's stage times are saved
While the agent's reply plays, speech detection hears you start; since the reply was reaching you, it isn't a turn yet, so a cough is passed over
Once frames judged speech add up to the interrupt speech, the listener says it's held: you've cut in, and your page is shown your words so far
The reply stops at once: conversation stops the model, text-to-speech stops, and no packet goes out after
The turn is saved cut: from the packets sent, the round trip and the browser's delay, the service works out how far you heard, to a whole word
Your page is told interrupted, with the reply as far as you heard it; what you go on to say is the next turn, whose prompt holds only that part
Your spoken turn has been taken: conversation holds it in flight while the reply's text streams and text-to-speech makes its first phrase
You start speaking again before any of the reply could have reached you, by the same estimate used for a cut
That's talking on: the reply stops, and your page is told so and shown that turn's words again, which your new words join
The service takes the turn back in conversation: it is removed as if never taken, so no prompt holds a reply you never heard
When you finish, all your words, old and new, are taken as one turn in its place, under the same request ID

nodes.name: Service
nodes.summary: Holds each session's audio connection, takes its turns, plays replies, cuts in, works out what was heard.
nodes.description: speech's use cases. It answers audio offers, one connection per session on a server, a newer one replacing the old, at most a set number per server, each ended when the ticket that opened it expires, a reply playing cut where heard and no turn taken from then, even while it closes; reads the data channel's turns in order, at most two waiting; takes spoken turns from what the listener notices once the end-of-turn check and the final text agree; hands every turn to conversation; streams the reply's text to the page and its audio to the track in real time; and when the user cuts in, stops the audio at once and saves the reply as far as it was heard.
nodes.why: The browser removes the agent's echo only from audio arriving over WebRTC, and interrupting needs the microphone open while the agent speaks.

nodes.name: Listener
nodes.summary: Per connection: notices speech, a pause, the maximum wait and speech held over the agent.
nodes.description: Domain logic, one per audio connection, made with its microphone's first audio: cuts the 16 kHz audio into 32 ms frames, keeps the last 8 s for the end-of-turn check, and notices speech starting, a 0.2 s pause, the 3 s maximum wait and 0.2 s of speech held over the agent, counting every length in the audio itself.
nodes.why: Judging speech on the server works the same for every client and is timed where the turn is timed.

nodes.name: Transport
nodes.summary: Sets up audio connections.
members: Connection: Play · Listen · Send · Messages · RoundTrip · Done · Close
nodes.description: The audio transport's swap point: Answer sets up a connection from a browser's offer. A Connection plays Opus packets, yields the microphone's 16 kHz audio, sends and receives data-channel messages, measures its round trip, and closes with a reason.

nodes.name: SpeechDetection
nodes.summary: A detector per connection, judging frames.
nodes.description: Speech detection's swap point: a Detector per audio connection gives each 32 ms frame the probability that it holds speech.
nodes.why: Speech detection runs in pure Go inside voice, so the build keeps no C library and needs no network hop.

nodes.name: SpeechToText
nodes.summary: Utterance audio in, rough then final text out.
nodes.description: Speech-to-text's swap point, a stream both ways: each utterance's audio in, its rough text each time it grows, then its final text or a failure.
nodes.why: Any service speaking the same realtime transcription API swaps in by setting.

nodes.name: EndOfTurn
nodes.summary: Has the user finished?
nodes.description: The end-of-turn check's swap point: whether the user has finished, judged from up to the last 8 s of 16 kHz audio.
nodes.why: A silence timer alone either cuts users off or feels slow; judging from the audio works with any speech-to-text.

nodes.name: TextToSpeech
nodes.summary: Reply text in, 20 ms Opus packets out.
nodes.description: Text-to-speech's swap point: reads the reply's text as the model streams it and yields 20 ms Opus packets, each marked with its phrase (its text, where it ends in the reply, its packet count), so how much was heard can be worked out.
nodes.why: Each phrase's packets mark where it ends in the reply, so after an interrupt voice knows how much was heard.

nodes.name: http
nodes.summary: Sets up and ends a session's audio connection, the way WHIP does.
nodes.description: Inbound adapter: POST /v1/sessions/{id}/audio takes the browser's SDP offer and answers 201 with the SDP answer and the connection's own address; DELETE there ends that connection and no other. Registered on the router, behind its check: the session's ticket, which reconnects as often as the session is live; an offer with a ticket expired by speech's own clock is answered ticket-expired.

nodes.name: transport/webrtc
nodes.summary: Pion: the agent's Opus track, the microphone decoded to 16 kHz, the data channel.
nodes.description: Outbound adapter implementing Transport with Pion: an Opus track for the agent's audio, stamped as RTP asks; the browser's microphone decoded in pure Go to 16 kHz in 20 ms stretches; the data channel the browser opens, with a size limit on messages. It takes audio only on the server's private and loopback addresses unless told others, on ports of its own for each connection or one UDP port they all share, and can write other addresses into the answer in place of its own, as a container with a published port needs.

nodes.name: detection/silero
nodes.summary: Silero VAD v5 in pure Go through govad; weights shared, a detector per connection.
nodes.description: Outbound adapter implementing SpeechDetection with Silero VAD's model run in pure Go by govad; its 1.2 MB of weights are loaded once and shared, each connection gets a detector of its own.

nodes.name: stt/realtime
nodes.summary: WebSocket client of the realtime transcription API; 16 → 24 kHz.
nodes.description: Outbound adapter implementing SpeechToText against any service speaking OpenAI's realtime transcription API. One WebSocket per audio connection, opened at its first speech and again after a failure; each utterance an item, its texts matched by the item's ID; audio resampled from 16 to 24 kHz; opening, each send and each final text with a deadline.

nodes.name: endofturn/smartturn
nodes.summary: Asks the speech-to-text service's check, one second at most.
nodes.description: Outbound adapter implementing EndOfTurn: POST /v1/turn/check with the audio as audio/L16, a one-second deadline, plain HTTP and the standard library only.

nodes.name: tts/kokoro
nodes.summary: Cuts the reply into phrases, asks the service for one at a time, unwraps Ogg into 20 ms packets.
nodes.description: Outbound adapter implementing TextToSpeech: the first phrase ends at punctuation once it holds four words, later ones are whole sentences; one phrase is asked for at a time and never more than one ahead; each phrase's audio is read whole so every packet carries its count; a phrase with no first audio within 5 s fails.

views.title: user context
views.lead: The smallest module: a core with one port, Items, implemented by a PostgreSQL store. It imports none of the other modules and only its own store touches its tables; conversation reaches it through its service, to load context and to save each session's summary.

flows.name: A session loads what the agent may know

steps.caption: A session starts: conversation asks user context to Load the kinds its agent declares, within 20,000 characters by default
Current reads the user's items of those kinds that no newer item replaces, newest first; session summaries only if this agent wrote them
In the declared order, Load keeps each whole item that fits what is left of the limit; one that doesn't is left out and the next is tried
Load returns the items it chose and the IDs it left out; conversation saves the chosen items' IDs with the new session

flows.name: A turn reads what its session loaded

steps.caption: Each turn, conversation asks Items for the context items its session loaded, by ID; a session that loaded none doesn't ask
ByID reads them for that workspace and user, even if replaced since, so the prompt stays the same from turn to turn
Items returns them in the order asked; an ID that isn't this user's fails as no such context item, just like one that doesn't exist
After a session ends, its summary job has the model write a summary, then calls SaveSummary with the user, agent, session and when it ended
SaveSummary refuses a summary missing any of those, or with empty content, and gives it a new UUIDv7 ID
AddSummary inserts it unless the session already has a summary; a job run twice gets the first one back and saves nothing
When the session's delivery runs, SessionSummary reads that summary, or a newer item that replaced it, for the product's server

nodes.name: Service
nodes.summary: Load: declared kinds, whole items within a limit. Items: by ID. SaveSummary, and SessionSummary to read one.
nodes.description: Load takes the kinds an agent declares, in its order, newest first within a kind, whole items only, within the character limit the caller sends, and reports the IDs it left out. Items reads a session's loaded items back by ID, in the order loaded, refusing another user's or workspace's. The kinds are profile and session_summary. SaveSummary saves a session's summary once per session, with the agent that wrote it, the session and when it ended; only that agent loads it, the latest session's first. SessionSummary reads a session's summary as it stands, for the session's delivery to its product.
nodes.why: An agent reads only the kinds it declares, whole items within a limit, so anyone reading its file can predict what it is told.

nodes.name: Items
nodes.summary: Where context items are kept.
nodes.description: The storage port: the user's current items of the given kinds, those no other item replaces, newest first, summaries only the agent's own; items by ID, replaced or not; a session's summary, added once per session; and that summary as it stands, the one saved or its correction.

nodes.name: store/postgres
nodes.summary: user_context.context_items, never edited; a change replaces an item.
nodes.description: Items in user context's own schema. A database trigger refuses any edit of an item, and a replacement points at the item it replaces, the same user and kind.
nodes.why: A context item is never edited: a change is a new item that replaces the old one, so a session's prompt never shifts under it.

views.title: agents
views.lead: Agent definitions and their versions. The catalog serves conversation the newest and exact versions; publishing, run by cmd/publish from the agent files, is the only way a version is written. agents imports neither conversation nor speech.

flows.name: A member publishes an agent file

steps.caption: A member runs scripts/publish.sh: cmd/publish has agentfile read each agents/<name>.md, a YAML settings block, then the persona
agentfile refuses an unknown setting, a file not named <name>.md, two files with one ID and a folder with no agent files: nothing is published
cmd/publish refuses an agent reading a kind user context doesn't hold, then calls Publish, which checks every agent before saving any
For each agent, Save adds the next version number, unless the newest version has the same SHA-256 hash of settings and persona
Publish returns each agent's version number and whether it is new, and cmd/publish logs it as published or unchanged

flows.name: A session starts on an agent's newest version

steps.caption: A product's server lists agents or starts a session: conversation asks the catalog for its workspace's Available agents
Available reads the newest version of each agent on every call, so a publish shows at once on every instance
The session starts on the newest version of the agent asked for, and keeps that version's number for its whole life

flows.name: A turn reads its session's exact version

steps.caption: Each turn, and the summary after the session ends, asks the catalog for the exact Version the session started on
The first time an instance asks for that version, the catalog reads it from the store
A saved version never changes, so the catalog keeps it in memory and answers every later ask for it without the database

nodes.name: Catalog
nodes.summary: Each workspace's newest versions on every request; exact versions kept in memory once read.
nodes.description: The agents one workspace owns, as the module offers them: Available reads the newest version of each on every request, so a publish shows without a restart; Version returns one exact version, read once and then served from memory for its own number and workspace.
nodes.why: Newest versions are read on every request, so a publish shows at once on every instance; exact versions never change, so they are kept in memory.

nodes.name: Publish
nodes.summary: Checks every agent first, then saves each as its next version if its content changed.
nodes.description: Checks every agent before saving any (settings, the context kinds it reads, the session context names it declares), then saves each as its next version only when its content hash differs from the newest version's.
nodes.why: Publishing from the agent file is a step of its own, never part of a start, and saves nothing until every agent passes its checks.

nodes.name: Versions
nodes.summary: Where versions are kept.
nodes.description: The storage port: the newest version of each agent, one exact version, and saving the next version unless the newest has the same hash; saves of one agent take turns, so no number is given twice.

nodes.name: agentfile
nodes.summary: Reads agents/<name>.md: a YAML settings block, then the persona.
nodes.description: Reads agent files: Markdown, one per agent, opening with a YAML settings block (ID, name, description, the context kinds it reads, the session context it expects, its summary instruction, who speaks first), the rest the persona sent to the model as written. Refuses unknown settings, misnamed files and two files with one ID.

nodes.name: store/postgres
nodes.summary: agent.agents and agent.agent_versions; versions never updated.
nodes.description: Versions in the agents module's own schema; a trigger refuses updates, deletes and truncation of versions, and saving locks the agent's row so saves at once never share a number.

nodes.name: cmd/publish
nodes.summary: Run by the workspace when an agent file changes.

nodes.name: agents/*.md
nodes.description: Each file's settings block names who opens the session (opens) and, if it wants one, its own model (model).

edges.detail: Also checks that every kind an agent reads is one user context holds, before reaching the database.

views.title: job runner
views.lead: Hexagonal like a module: the runner holds the rules and declares one port, Store, the queue, implemented by a PostgreSQL store. It imports no module: cmd/voice hands each runner its kinds' handlers, and runs two, one for conversation's session summaries and one for its deliveries to products' servers.

steps.caption: Ending a session queues its summary job in the same write, and a delivery job to run after it when the workspace has a webhook
cmd/voice gives each instance two runners, each claiming only its own kinds: summaries on one worker, deliveries on four
Checking each second when idle, the summaries' runner claims the job due soonest, skipping rows another claim holds, on a one-minute lease
The runner decodes the job's args and runs its handler, which calls Summarize, for at most 30 seconds
Summarize succeeded, so Done marks the job done, saved only while this run still holds it, and the worker claims the next at once
Summarize fails, say the model doesn't answer, or returns busy because the model service is at its own cap
A failure is retried after 10 s, then 40 s, 160 s and 640 s: 5 runs for a summary, about 14 minutes; 8 for a delivery
After the last run, or args that don't decode, Fail ends the job for good; failed jobs stay in the table to be looked into
A busy run is let go with Release, not counted, and is due again 5 to 10 s later; voice stopping lets each job in hand go the same way
If an instance dies mid-run, the lease runs out after a minute and another runner claims the job
As voice starts and then every hour, cmd/voice has each runner Prune its own kinds
Prune deletes that runner's jobs done at least 7 days ago, across every workspace; failed jobs stay

nodes.name: Runner
nodes.summary: Claims the job due soonest of its own kinds, runs it with its handler, then done, retry, fail or let go.
nodes.description: Each runner runs Workers workers; each claims the job due soonest that no run holds, of the kinds the runner has handlers for, for a lease longer than a run's timeout, decodes its inputs into the kind's own Go type and runs the handler. A failed run waits and runs again, four times longer each time up to a day, until the job is done or out of the runner's attempts; a failure no later run would avoid fails at once; a run that found what it needs busy is let go without counting; stopping lets each job in hand go to run again. Prune deletes only its own kinds' jobs done, once past its own keeping time; failed ones stay.
nodes.why: Each instance runs a runner per group of kinds, claiming only its own, so one slow group holds up no other.

nodes.name: Store
nodes.summary: The queue.
nodes.description: The queue's port: claim the job due soonest that no run holds, of the kinds asked for, for a lease; mark it done, due again after a wait, failed for good, or let go without counting the run; delete jobs done long ago. A run's result is saved only by the run that holds the job.

nodes.name: store/postgres
nodes.summary: The jobs table: claims skip locked rows, so two instances never take one job.
nodes.description: Keeps the queue in the jobs table, through sqlc-generated queries. A claim takes the waiting job due soonest of the kinds asked for with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and moves its due time a lease ahead, so another instance takes it only once the lease runs out. A job queued to run after another is passed over while that one is still waiting, retries included. Claiming and pruning are the system's own sweeps, across workspaces: the claim reads out only the job it takes, and pruning reads nothing out.
nodes.why: Claims skip rows another claim holds, so any number of instances share one queue with no job run twice at once.

nodes.name: cmd/voice
nodes.summary: Registers each kind's handler; runs and prunes.

nodes.summary: Queues summary and delivery jobs; Summarize and Deliver run them.

views.title: product keys
views.lead: Hexagonal like a module: Keys holds the rules and declares one port, Store, implemented by a PostgreSQL store. The router asks Keys which workspace a key acts for; cmd/productkey makes, lists and revokes keys. Only each key's hash is kept.

flows.name: A product's server is let in

steps.caption: A product's server sends its product key as a Bearer credential to list agents, start or end a session; the vgk_ prefix tells the router it is one
The router refuses a product key on a route that takes only a ticket, and any sent from a page, with an Origin header, without checking it
The router asks Keys for the key's Workspace; Keys answers unknown for a key of the wrong length or form without asking the store
Keys hashes it with SHA-256, and the store finds the working key with that hash across workspaces: the key itself names the workspace
Found, the request goes on as that workspace's product; an unknown or revoked key gets 401, a check that couldn't be made 503, to retry

flows.name: A member makes a product key

steps.caption: A member runs scripts/product-key.sh create, and cmd/productkey asks Keys to Create a key for the workspace
Create makes vgk_ plus 32 random bytes in base64url, and keeps only the key's SHA-256 and its first 12 characters
Add saves that record, with a new UUIDv7 ID, in the product_keys table
cmd/productkey prints the key, the only time it is shown; everywhere else a Key prints, logs and encodes as redacted

flows.name: A member lists and revokes product keys

steps.caption: list shows the workspace's keys, newest first: each one's ID, first characters, when it was made and whether it is revoked
revoke ID asks Keys to Revoke that key of the workspace; an ID the workspace doesn't have is refused
The store sets the key's revoked time, so every check from now on refuses it, then counts the keys still working
cmd/productkey confirms, and warns when no working key is left: every start from the product is then refused until one is made

nodes.name: Keys
nodes.summary: Makes a key, checks one by its hash, lists and revokes; a Key prints and logs redacted.
nodes.description: Create makes a key, vgk_ and 256 random bits in base64url, and keeps its SHA-256 and first 12 characters; the key is returned once, held in a Key that formats, logs and encodes redacted, behind a pointer. Workspace refuses a malformed key without a read, then finds the hash among the working keys: unknown, revoked and malformed look alike, and a store that can't answer is a failure, never unknown. Revoke stops a key at once and counts the keys still working.
nodes.why: A key is kept only as its SHA-256 and found by that hash, since the key itself names its workspace.

nodes.name: Store
nodes.summary: Where what is kept of each key lives.
nodes.description: The port for what is kept of product keys: add a record, find the workspace of the working key with a hash, list a workspace's keys newest first, revoke one keeping the first revoke time, and count a workspace's working keys.

nodes.name: store/postgres
nodes.summary: The product_keys table: a key found by its hash, across workspaces.
nodes.description: Keeps the records in the product_keys table through sqlc-generated queries. Finding a key by its hash looks across workspaces, since the key is what names the workspace, and reads out only that workspace; listing, revoking and counting name the workspace.
